Jim stood in the back of the studio, his neck craned so far forward he looked less like a human being and more like a confused giraffe trying to spot a leaf on a high branch. He had intended to join the "Gentle Stretching for Beginners" class, but a misread flyer and a severe case of directional dyslexia had landed him in "Advanced Vinyasa Flow: The Pain Zone."

The instructor, a serene woman named Serenity who looked like she hadn’t blinked since 1998, glided over. "Jim," she whispered, her voice like wind chimes in a library. "You are here for the Camel Pose. Ustrasana."

Jim nodded vigorously, his long neck bobbing like a buoy in a storm. "Right. Camel. Got it. I’m basically a camel. I have the hump. Well, not the hump, but the neck. I’m very neck-forward."

Serenity smiled tightly. "Breathe. Arch back. Reach for your heels."

Jim attempted to arch his back. However, because he was a yoga novice with the flexibility of a wet noodle and the core strength of a jellyfish, his spine didn’t arch so much as it crumpled. As he leaned back, his center of gravity betrayed him. He didn’t reach for his heels; he reached for the floor, but his hands were too short, so he ended up grabbing his own ankles in a desperate, flailing grip.

The strain was immense. Jim’s face turned the color of a ripe tomato. He squeezed his eyes shut, focusing all his energy on not falling over. This intense internal pressure, combined with the fact that he had eaten a large bean burrito for lunch, created a perfect storm of biological pressure.

*Pfft.*

It was a small sound, barely audible over the ambient singing bowl music. But in the silent, zen-filled room, it echoed like a gunshot.

Serenity froze mid-pose. The woman next to Jim, who was currently balancing on one leg in a complex eagle pose, opened one eye.

Jim, unaware of the acoustic disaster, grunted. "Hnnngh! Almost... there!"

He pushed harder.

*Toot-toot.*

This time, it was longer. It had a distinct vibrato.
